name: Ernest Dowson
bio: English poet of the Decadence and one of the Rhymers' Club - the loose association of young poets, meeting at the Cheshire Cheese in Fleet Street, whose two Books of the Rhymers' Club (1892, 1894) carried his work alongside Yeats, Lionel Johnson and Arthur Symons. He met Wilde in 1890 and, with Robert Sherard, visited him at Oakley Street 'in the dark days between his trials'. Living at Arques-la-Bataille near Dieppe in the summer of 1897, he was among the first friends to reach Wilde after his release, dining at Berneval on 3 June and seeing him constantly until his own return to London in mid-July; the twelve surviving letters from Wilde to him are the largest cluster of the Berneval/Dieppe months, and travel from 'Cher Monsieur le Poete' to 'Tout a toi'. Frankel calls him at this period 'one of his closest confidantes' and credits the friendship - together with Wilde's reading of A. E. Housman - as a spur to the composition of The Ballad of Reading Gaol. The correspondence resumed from Naples that October, by then largely about a debt of some 18-20 pounds Dowson owed Wilde; he died at Robert Sherard's house at Catford on 23 February 1900, nine months before Wilde, who asked Smithers to put flowers on his grave.
bio_note: DATES (established so far, 2026-08-03): born 1867, died 23 February 1900. The year-pair is from the editors' main-particulars footnote at Dowson's first appearance in the text - Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), printed p. 877 n. 1 (repo PDF 927): 'English poet (1867-1900). He had met Wilde in 1890 and with Robert Sherard visited him at Oakley Street in the dark days between his trials.' The exact death date is from the editors' footnote to Wilde's letter of condolence to Smithers, printed p. 1173 n. 2 (repo PDF 1219): 'Ernest Dowson died in Robert Sherard's house at Catford on 23 February 1900. He was buried in the Roman Catholic part of Lewisham Cemetery on 27 February.' No birth month or day is given by any source read so far, so none is recorded. Both pages were located in the OCR text mirror, then read as rendered page images with the printed folio confirmed at the foot. BIO SOURCING: the Rhymers' Club membership from the editors' footnote at Complete Letters printed p. 422 n. 2 (repo PDF 444, OCR mirror only, unverified in the source), which names the Cheshire Cheese meetings and the two Books of the Rhymers' Club (1892, 1894) with 'W. B. Yeats, Lionel Johnson, Ernest Dowson, Arthur Symons' among the contributors. The 1890 meeting and the Oakley Street visit between the trials from printed p. 877 n. 1 as above (independently asserted, without Sherard, at Sox, Bachelors of Art (1991), printed p. 141). The Berneval/Dieppe period from Wilde's letters at printed pp. 877-926 and from Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), printed p. 113 (repo PDF 127, folio confirmed on the rendered page): Dowson 'now one of his closest confidantes, whom Wilde had known back in London and who resided near Dieppe, at Arques-la-Bataille, until his departure for London in mid-July'; the Ballad claim at Frankel printed p. 121 (repo PDF 135, OCR/text layer). The Naples debt from Wilde to Dowson, printed pp. 957, 965, 969, 971. Frankel's 'just nine months before his own' at printed p. 114 (repo PDF 128, folio confirmed on the rendered page). NOT RECORDED AS A CONTEXT ENGAGEMENT, but on the record: Fothergill, in his unpublished memoir as printed by Sox at p. 141, 'commented that Dowson was in love with the owner of the Cafe Royal, but was "faithful only after his fashion"'; and the Complete Letters editors, glossing Wilde's otherwise 'inexplicable' 1898 reference to a 'Mrs Dowson' (printed p. 1018 n. 3), note that 'Ernest Dowson never married and his mother had died in 1895' and read the phrase as 'probably a reference to a newly acquired mistress or one of the prostitutes whose company he enjoyed'. Neither person is on the roster and neither is named, so neither gets a marker. Full passages, page-by-page provenance and the pagination table in dossiers/DOWSON_dossier.md.
